title: Bresson’s Pursuit of Cinematic Verity
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/ena-alvarado
text:
A filmmaker friend once told me that, as an older man, Robert Bresson insisted he no longer frequented the cinema. None of the new pictures were worth his time. Smelling a sham, the editorial staff of the distinguished French film journal Cahiers du cinéma hired a private detective to trail his footsteps. Not only was Bresson going to the theater, but he was also watching everything, kung-fu movies included.

True or not, the anecdote says more about the legendary magazine than the legendary director. From film theorist André Bazin to nouvelle vague darling Jean-Luc Godard, the influential French critics of the 1950s worshipped Bresson. (“He is the French cinema, as Dostoevsky is the Russian novel and Mozart is German music,” Godard once said.) Their journal laid the foundation for the importance of his work across generations of film enthusiasts.

By contrast, the response of the general public to Bresson’s films was often tepid, probably reflecting its ambivalence about the very minimalism that stimulated such debate about his filmography during the last century—until a certain consensus emerged.

Bresson’s filmmaking, the common refrain now goes, is concerned with the spiritual. The publication of Paul Schrader’s greatly influential Transcendental Style in Film: Ozu, Bresson, Dreyer, in 1972, helped establish this view. Schrader, a former Calvinist, went so far as to suggest the Bressonian project was essentially a Jansenist one. (Never mind that Bresson himself considered it “madness” to be “called a Jansenist.”) As philosopher Robert B. Pippin argues in his newest book, Robert Bresson: Cinematic Style as Philosophy, even critics who have stopped short of identifying Bresson as an overtly Catholic auteur still believe that his films are primarily “vehicles for the expression of his own religious commitments,” however orthodox or heterodox those religious commitments may be.

Pippin, a professor at the University of Chicago and the longtime chair of its Committee on Social Thought, is principally known for his scholarship on Kant and Hegel. In recent years, his work has delved more and more into cinema, with books on Howard Hawks, John Ford, Alfred Hitchcock, and Douglas Sirk. Robert Bresson marks his first foray outside of Hollywood. It also constitutes a refreshing and much-needed attempt at shaping “an alternate interpretation of Bresson’s enterprise” grounded in this realm, as opposed to a transcendental one.

In an effort to illustrate how and why Bresson’s “films should be understood as a form of philosophical thought,” Pippin analyzes his distinct style and closely probes a selection of his oeuvre, including Diary of a Country Priest (1951), Pickpocket (1959), Au hasard Balthazar (1966), Mouchette (1967), and L’Argent (1983).

Any appraisal of Bresson’s films must contend with the cinematic techniques that he so distinctively and stubbornly deployed. Like Kant and Hegel, who pursued comprehensive philosophical systems, Bresson developed a totalizing theory of filmmaking that informed nearly all thirteen of the feature films he directed over the course of his forty-year career. Additionally, he famously explained his unique system in Notes on the Cinematograph, a short book of aphorisms first published in 1975.

As Pippin observes, Bresson believed that cinema “can disclose something about human beings that cannot be disclosed otherwise,” though only if it makes full use of “the medium-specific capacities of the art,” which, in his view, most films had failed to do. For Bresson, those films were specimens of a derivative art more accurately described as “filmed theater.” The problem mainly stemmed from professional acting. A star like Leonardo DiCaprio implicitly tells viewers, in Bresson’s words, “It’s not me you are seeing and hearing, it’s the other man”—as in, it’s Titanic’s Jack Dawson. Yet, as Pippin explains, Bresson believed Leo and Jack inevitably appear together onscreen, since “it is impossible to submerge the former into the latter; we always see both.” 

Additionally, actors’ expressionistic performances make their characters’ inner worlds more palpable to viewers than humans actually are to one another in real life. This produces the effect of falseness, spectacle, theater. It also leaves little room for interpretation and imagination, since viewers are so clearly shown what to think. According to Bresson, his project was this: 

Not to shoot a film in order to illustrate a thesis, or to display men and women confined to their external aspect, but to discover the matter they are made of. To attain that “heart of the heart” which does not let itself be caught either by poetry, or by philosophy, or by drama.

In other words, Bresson wished to capture whatever was “uniquely, if also indirectly and elliptically, available to the camera and the sound recorder.” To that end, he cast nonprofessionals, whom he dubbed “models.” (It might be helpful to think of the people who pose for painters as analogous.) Instead of directing models to act, Bresson guided them to behave in front of the camera. This principally involved asking models to repeat each scene so many times that they would eventually deliver the lines and carry out the scripted gestures entirely thoughtlessly. In Bresson’s estimation, “Nine-tenths of our movements obey habit and automatism,” and that meant it “is anti-nature to subordinate them to will and to thought.” His goal was to suppress visible intentionality.

Pippin argues that this choice reveals a great deal about Bresson’s philosophical commitments. His disdain for actors indicated his disbelief “that actions we perform are always best understood by reference to the intentions we would self-consciously avow,” however sincere those avowals might be. Instead, models’ automatic acts disclose hints of their real motivations. For this reason, absent self-reflection and other traditional “markers of a character’s identity,” Bresson’s films must rely on what Pippin recognizes as the “formal means unique in cinema, one where the barest hint of a reaction, a motorcycle ride, a long moment of silence, the slow, patient, carrying out of [a] task, a hand on a seat, a moment in a church, a counterfeit bill, all by virtue of this minimalism, carry a weight of possible meaning that is absent in conventional cinema.”

For many, this minimalism—at least upon initial contact—feels uncomfortably bare and austere. It jolts the audience. In Pippin’s view, the fact that Bresson’s films strike us as “mysterious, opaque, elusive” means they require “what existence itself requires,” namely, “attempts at interpretation.” As he writes, “Rather than withholding anything, Bresson is attesting to how little can ever be known about a character, even by the character him- or herself, that the basic condition of human interchange is unknowingness and at best uncertainty.”

Complicating this picture, Pippin insists that the world, with its people and objects, is nevertheless potentially meaningful, only in a nondiscursive and even precognitive way. This presentation of experience is, for him, “the most fundamental feature of Bresson’s cinematic innovations.” He relates Bresson’s invitation to feel rather than understand in the pursuit of meaning to Heidegger’s idea of “attunement” or “mood” (in German, Stimmung)—or, the way things “offer themselves to our grasp.” For both Heidegger and Bresson, the mood of our modern, Western world is one of profound boredom. As individuals, we cannot control or change this mood, because we are born or “simply ‘thrown’” into a “particular historical world.”

The particular historical world of Bresson’s films was postwar France, a country recovering from the deadliest war in human history and entering a period of rapid technological change. It offered people, including Bresson’s characters, a “paucity of available sources of mattering,” but “not because of any general, inescapable sinfulness.”

Almost thirty years after his death, what has become of Bresson’s vision of cinema? He repeatedly called his works “cinematographs” rather than movies, because they took such a radically different path from the one the filmmaking industry at large ultimately settled on. As Pippin notes, when watching films, we “think of ourselves as observing unobserved, invisible, and thereby onto some truth, not what would be pretended if we were acknowledged. But this is the illusion of reality, the great trick of traditional cinema, and it encourages laziness and passivity on the part of the viewer.” From this perspective, directors who demand truly active participation from us might be understood as following Bresson’s seldom-trodden track. Filmmakers as different as the Chinese documentarian Wang Bing, the Austrian iconoclast Michael Haneke, and the Argentine cinephile-turned-director María Aparicio all count as formidable candidates. Wang’s multi-hour portraits of factory workers rely on monotonous repetition to capture the mood of state capitalism. Haneke’s use of montage is, like Bresson’s, austere and unexpected in an effort to rid viewers of narrative expectations, while Aparicio imbues objects with unexpressed meaning. 

Despite its depth and seriousness, Pippin’s provocative book is compromised by flagrant copyediting errors that give the sense of a work in progress rather than a finished monograph. I stopped keeping track of the number of duplicate sentences: On pages 61 and 67, for instance, we learn, twice, that the atmosphere of Bresson’s films “is suffused with an arid lifelessness, an existential deadness in which anything one can do that can create an erotic (or any other kind of) frisson, life, energy, danger, thrill, is shown to be irresistible.” (I confirmed with the University of Chicago Press that I had a final copy, not a galley, in my hands.) In his conclusion, Pippin remarks that he tried “to identify as a major focus of Bresson’s films the problem of meaningfulness” by alluding to Elle in Une femme douce and Charles in The Devil, Probably—two characters and films that are not discussed (or, in the case of Elle, even mentioned) in his book.

These slips are perhaps symptomatic of a deeper problem. Pippin’s original ideas—the ones that make up the core of his book, which I have tried to summarize—are carefully and closely fleshed out in the first two chapters, comprising the introduction on Bresson’s methods and his reading of Diary of a Country Priest. Yet each successive chapter becomes shorter in length and thinner in argumentation, like a March of Progress in reverse. One wonders if what Pippin has turned into a book could have worked better as a single scholarly article.

Still, to see with new eyes a canonized artist’s work, to inject freshness into otherwise deadened discourse, is no easy matter. This is Robert Bresson’s saving grace: Pippin’s convincing claim that it “is the meaningfulness of this world (or its unfulfilled or failed possibility) that Bresson wants to return us to, make us attentive to, not escape.”
